The Round-tailed ground squirrel (Xerospermophilus tereticaudus) is a small-bodied scintid inhabiting the arid deserts of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Neonates emerge from a gestation period remarkably brief for a mammal of this lineage, with field observations indicating a gestation time of 28 days [tg = 28 days] when maternal body temperatures average 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of the species' active period during the hot season. Newborn pups are altricial and remarkably diminutive, with a recorded wet weight at birth of just 3.9 grams [Wwb = 3.9 grams] at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a value that represents roughly 2.4 percent of the mass of an average adult female. This minimal neonatal mass imposes considerable maternal investment during the subsequent lactation phase, as the offspring must more than double in size repeatedly to reach nutritional independence. The species exhibits a comparatively rapid developmental schedule, and the brief gestation time of 28 days [tg = 28 days] at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C] aligns with the fast life-history strategy predicted for small desert mammals facing short windows of resource abundance.

Lactation and maternal care proceed over a defined period before the pups are capable of independent foraging. Under the typical thermal conditions of the species' active season, the time since birth at weaning has been measured at 39 days [tx = 39 days] at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], reflecting the rapid somatic development necessary to escape maternal dependence before the onset of the most extreme summer heat. By this stage, the nursing offspring attain a wet weight at weaning of approximately 75 grams [Wwx = approximately 75 grams], representing a nearly twenty-fold increase from the scant 3.9 gram [Wwb = 3.9 gram] mass recorded at parturition. This accelerated growth trajectory is typical of ground squirrel species that inhabit unpredictable environments where early independence confers a survival advantage. Weaning marks a critical transition, as the young must begin to accumulate sufficient body reserves for their first winter torpor, all while navigating the physiological challenges of a desert landscape. Weaning at this 39-day mark (39 days after birth) [tx = 39 days after birth], measured at 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], enables the young to begin foraging independently before the peak of summer aridity.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs over a considerably longer timescale than the early developmental stages. Available data indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 325 days [tp = approximately 325 days] under the typical body temperature range of roughly 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], meaning that young squirrels born in the spring of one year will generally become reproductively competent by the following spring reproductive season. This interval encompasses a full cycle of active foraging, hibernation, and post-emergence conditioning, suggesting that attainment of a critical body mass threshold is necessary before gonadal activation can occur. The ultimate wet weight of a fully mature adult has been recorded at 163.3 grams [Wwi = 163.3 grams], a mass that females typically achieve by their second active season. Males and females are broadly similar in size, though slight sexual dimorphism has been noted in some populations. At a typical body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], this species reaches sexual maturity at approximately 325 days [tp = approximately 325 days] of age, a pace that places it among the faster-maturing members of the genus Xerospermophilus, a life-history trait likely linked to high adult mortality rates from predation and environmental extremes.

Reproductive output is tightly constrained by the desert environment and the need to compress breeding into a narrow seasonal window. Females produce a single litter per year, and the maximum reproductive rate observed in wild populations has been quantified at 5.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.4 pups per litter], with a reproductive frequency of one litter annually [F_R_i = one litter annually] under the body temperature conditions of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C] typical of an active, normothermic individual. This litter size represents the upper bound of fecundity, with mean values often lower in years of poor forage availability or following harsh winters. The combination of moderate litter size and single annual reproduction yields a conservative annual reproductive output compared to small rodents from more mesic environments. However, the 5.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.4 pups per litter] observed at 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C] suggests that when thermal and nutritional conditions are optimal, females can channel substantial resources into offspring production. The duration of lactation, maternal den attendance, and the necessity of bringing young to a weaning mass of 75 grams [Wwx = 75 grams] collectively impose a heavy energetic burden that limits the possibility of a second annual litter.

Longevity data for the Round-tailed ground squirrel remain somewhat uncertain, but the best available estimates place the maximum lifespan at approximately 8.9 years [am = approximately 8.9 years] at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a figure derived from mark-recapture studies in Arizona. This lifespan, while modest by mammalian standards, is relatively long for a small-bodied scintid, reflecting the protective benefits of hibernation during the winter months and a burrowing lifestyle that mitigates predation risk. The uncertainty surrounding this estimate stems from the difficulty of tracking individuals across multiple years in low-density desert populations and the challenges of distinguishing senescence from environmentally induced mortality. Reaching an ultimate wet weight of 163.3 grams [Wwi = 163.3 grams] by adulthood, individuals of this species trade off rapid early growth against a moderately extended reproductive lifespan. A maximal documented survival of 8.9 years [am = 8.9 years] at 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C] allows multiple breeding seasons, though few individuals likely survive to this upper limit. The interplay between a remarkably short gestational phase lasting just 28 days [tg = 28 days] at 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C] and an extended potential lifespan underscores the flexible life-history strategy that enables this species to persist in one of North America's most thermally challenging habitats.
